title: Durable vs Transient Subscriptions
description: Learn the difference between durable and transient subscriptions and when to use each for reliable messaging.

data.text: When a consumer subscribes to a message queue, it chooses between a **durable** and **transient** (non-durable) subscription. This choice determines whether the queue — and by extension the subscription — survives a broker restart. Durable subscriptions are the backbone of reliable messaging systems, while transient subscriptions are useful for short-lived consumers like background workers or ad-hoc listeners.

A durable subscription requires two conditions: (1) the queue itself must be declared as `durable: true`, and (2) the exchange that feeds it must also be durable. A transient subscription uses an `exclusive` or `auto-delete` queue, which the broker removes when the consumer disconnects. Broker restarts wipe auto-delete queues, along with any messages stored inside them.

data.title: Auto-Delete Is Not Durable
data.text: Declaring a queue with auto-delete means the broker removes it when the last consumer unsubscribes. This is convenient for temporary workers but dangerous if you expect messages to survive a crash. Always double-check queue arguments when configuring production consumers.

data.caption: Durable vs transient subscription lifecycle across broker restarts
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Publisher
    participant E as Exchange
    participant Q as Queue
    participant C as Consumer
    participant B as Broker

    P->>E: Publish message
    E->>Q: Route to durable queue
    Q->>Q: Message persists on disk

    Note over B: Broker restarts
    B->>Q: Durable queue restored
    Q->>C: Consumer reconnects
    C->>Q: Message still available

    P->>E: Publish to transient queue
    E->>Q: Route to auto-delete queue
    Note over B: Broker restarts
    B->>Q: Queue deleted; messages lost

data.text: Durable subscriptions are the foundation of reliable messaging architectures. In financial systems, healthcare, and e-commerce, losing a message during a broker restart can result in data loss, missed transactions, or compliance violations. Always use durable queues for these workloads and pair them with publisher confirms to ensure messages reach the broker before the publisher continues.

Transient subscriptions are not without value. They are ideal for request-reply patterns, health-check consumers, and real-time dashboards where a brief data gap during a restart is acceptable. The shorter lifecycle also means fewer resources are consumed on the broker. However, always document which queues are transient so that other engineers do not assume messages are being retained.
The following C# example contrasts a durable subscription with a transient one. The key difference is the `durable` and `exclusive` flags passed when declaring the queue.

terms.definition: A subscription backed by a durable queue that survives broker restarts and replays unacknowledged messages to reconnected consumers.
A subscription backed by an exclusive, auto-delete queue that is removed when the consumer disconnects.
A queue property that causes the broker to delete the queue when its last consumer unsubscribes.
A queue that can be consumed by only one connection. When that connection closes, the queue is deleted.

data.title: Exercise: Choose the Right Subscription Type
data.description: For each scenario below, decide whether a durable or transient subscription is most appropriate, and justify your choice.
steps: An order processing service that must not lose any order events across broker restarts.
A request-reply pattern where a client sends a query and waits for one response.
A real-time dashboard that shows live metrics and can tolerate missing data points during a restart.
An audit service that archives every message for compliance purposes.
data.expectedOutcome: A short justification for each scenario showing understanding of durability guarantees and failure modes.

items.question: Can I declare a queue as durable in code but the broker discards it anyway?
items.answer: Yes, if the exchange it is bound to is not also declared durable. Both the exchange and queue must be durable for messages to survive a broker restart.

items.question: What is the difference between exclusive and auto-delete?
items.answer: Exclusive means only one connection can consume from the queue. Auto-delete means the queue is deleted when its last consumer unsubscribes. A queue can be exclusive without auto-delete, or auto-delete without exclusive.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Durable subscriptions survive broker restarts; transient ones do not.
Both the exchange and queue must be durable for message persistence.
Transient queues are useful for RPC replies and short-lived consumers.
Always configure DLQs on durable queues to handle undeliverable messages.
